title: The sky is falling
hook: a hare hears a fruit fall and starts a stampede; a lion checks the facts (Jataka 322)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the preacher of khanti, patience no blade could reach. Your line: patience holds. Today, a noise in the forest.

Thud. A hare is lying under a palm tree, near a grove of vilva trees, turning over an anxious thought: if the earth broke apart, what would become of me? Just then a ripe vilva fruit drops onto a dry palm leaf right beside him. Thud. He doesn't look round to see what it was. He's already running, and shouting as he goes. The old saying has the sky falling. In this Jataka tale, it's the earth.
screen: `AN ANXIOUS HARE.` → `A FRUIT DROPS ON A LEAF.` → `HE RUNS WITHOUT LOOKING.`

segments.voice: First, the run. The hare cries that the earth is breaking up. Another hare sees him running and runs too, without asking why. Then more hares, then deer and boars, buffaloes and tigers, even elephants, a whole forest pounding toward the sea. Second, the lion. A lion sees the stampede and asks the one question nobody has asked: who saw the earth breaking up? The elephants don't know; the tigers told them. The tigers point to others, and so on down the line, back to the hares, and the hares point at one hare. Third, the check. Where were you when you heard it, the lion asks. He takes the hare on his back and goes to the spot. There's the palm leaf, and the fruit lying on it. Fourth, the return. The lion goes back and tells the herd what he found, and the animals, who were running toward the sea, are saved. In the tale the lion is the Buddha in an earlier life, and his gift is not strength or speed: one question, and the patience to walk back and look. A frightening thing passes from mouth to mouth and grows as it goes. Everyone runs because someone else is running. Nobody goes back to the palm leaf.
screen: `THE WHOLE FOREST RUNS.` · `WHO SAW IT?` · `BACK TO THE PALM LEAF.` · `THE HERD IS SAVED.` · then, large: `CHECK FIRST.`

segments.voice: Let the mind bring up one worry it's picked up from somewhere, passed along, half-heard, shared without a source, and watch how fast it wants to run. Then ask the lion's question: who saw it, and where's the palm leaf? No answer is needed now; just feel the difference between a thud and a falling world.
Palm leaf. What a lion found at the bottom of a rumor, a hare's fruit fallen onto a dry palm leaf, after the whole forest stampeded toward the sea. Today's word.
Your line: check first. The week in lines: an act of truth, don't look back, careful what you revive, the bray gives it away, help anyway, patience holds, check first. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhist teaching on right speech asks whether words are true, helpful and timely before they're spoken, and teachers sometimes use this tale to show how a rumor grows.

fork.setup: you're the lion, and the whole forest is stampeding past you toward the sea. what do you do?
options: run with them; they must know something.
ask who saw it, and go back to look.
roar to make them run faster.
fork.reveal: the lion traces the story back to one hare, carries him to the spot, finds the fruit on the palm leaf, and saves the herd.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nursery tale about panic.
what it means: one unchecked sound becomes a stampede, and one question stops it.
what a scholar hears: in the Jataka the hare fears the earth breaking up, not the sky, and the lion who checks is the Bodhisatta.
recall: the steady chant for reciting verses
guess: the small true cause behind a big scare
a sign that the earth is breaking up
a message passed from one hare to the next

chat.says: In the hare story, how did the lion stop the whole stampede?
options: He asked who saw it, traced it back, and went to look at the spot.
He roared so loudly that every animal froze and stopped running.
He told them the earth was fine, and they trusted the king of beasts.
chat.meaning: The lion asked who saw the earth breaking, traced the story back to one hare, and went to the palm leaf. Checking saved the herd.

vilva.meaning: a fruit tree; its ripe fruit fell on the palm leaf

Jataka.meaning: the collection of stories of the Buddha's past lives
